summary: Describes a Vendor-Specific LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF), allowing organizations to use implementation-specific encodings for LCAF addresses. It updates RFC 8060. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: A shared address format sometimes is not enough. This gives companies a private slot, with their ID on it, to write addresses in their own way.

questions: how can vendors define custom lisp address formats
what happens to unrecognized lcaf types
what is an oui in lisp
subtitle: A private slot in LISP's address format where vendors can encode addresses their own way.

tldr.problem: Some LISP deployments need address encodings that only make sense for one use case, and the shared LCAF types do not cover them. RFC 8060 also does not say what to do with an LCAF type it does not recognize.
tldr.mechanism: It defines the Vendor-Specific LCAF (Type 255), which carries a 24-bit IEEE OUI followed by a vendor-defined internal format. It also says unrecognized LCAF types MUST be ignored.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can define their own LCAF encodings, but the type SHOULD NOT be used where different organizations interoperate.

today: RFC 9306 is an Experimental specification published in October 2022. It updates RFC 8060 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why a Vendor-Specific LCAF
sections.content:
The LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF) in RFC 8060 defines formats and encodings for address types used in deployments of the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP). Some deployments need encodings that are not applicable outside the use case they were defined for.

RFC 9306 therefore adds a Vendor-Specific LCAF that lets organizations create LCAF addresses used only on particular LISP implementations. It also updates RFC 8060 to say how to treat unrecognized LCAF types.
sections.eli5: Most people share one address book format. Sometimes a company needs a special page that only its own computers understand, and this gives it one.

sections.title: Handling Unrecognized LCAF Types
sections.content:
RFC 8060 did not explain what to do with an LCAF type an implementation does not recognize. RFC 9306 says any unrecognized LCAF type received in a LISP control plane message MUST be ignored.

If that leaves no Locators, the result is the same as a control message with Locator Count = 0. If an EID-Prefix contains only unrecognized LCAF types, the control message MUST be dropped and the event MUST be logged.
sections.eli5: If you get a note written in a code you do not know, you skip it. If the whole note is in that code, you throw it away and write down that it happened.

sections.title: The Vendor-Specific LCAF Format
sections.content:
The first 8 octets are the general LCAF fields from RFC 8060: AFI = 16387, Rsvd1, Flags, Type = 255, Rsvd2 and Length. The Type MUST be 255, the value IANA assigned. Length covers the internal format, the OUI and the Rsvd3 field.

Three fields follow. Rsvd3 is 8 bits, MUST be 0 on transmit and MUST be ignored on receipt. The OUI is a 24-bit Organizationally Unique Identifier or Company ID assigned by the IEEE Registration Authority, which prevents collisions between vendors. The internal format is variable length and deliberately left undefined, so each vendor defines its own.
sections.eli5: The label always says 'special company page.' Next comes the company's own ID number, then whatever the company wants to write.

sections.title: Interoperability and Security
sections.content:
The Vendor-Specific LCAF type SHOULD NOT be used in deployments where different organizations interoperate. Where organizations do explicitly and mutually agree to use one, they need to carefully assess the interoperability concerns. Using an OUI not assigned to the organization is NOT RECOMMENDED.

A LISP device that receives a Vendor-Specific LCAF with an OUI it does not understand MUST drop the message and SHOULD create a log message. For security, each organization is responsible for assessing the formats it defines, and the security considerations of RFC 8060 apply.
sections.eli5: Private pages are fine inside one company. If another company's computer sees an ID it does not know, it drops the note.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Internal format plus OUI plus Rsvd3.

fields.name: Rsvd3
fields.desc: Reserved; 0 on transmit, ignored on receipt.
